items.title: We’re not going to win by lobbying, plotting, or manipulating. We’re going to win by building, in th...
items.content:
We’re not going to win by lobbying, plotting, or manipulating. We’re going to win by building, in the open, with the whole community!

Today, with @ggerganov we’re super excited to announce the release of llama.cpp v1, the first major fully stable version of the most used library to run AI models locally, meaning on your phone, your laptop, and your workstation.

It means you can own your intelligence for free, not send your data to anyone and be 100% in control, wherever you are in the world. It shows our commitment to support every hardware, platform and model type out there and makes AI distributed rather than concentrated in a few Silicon Valley orgs.

Huge thanks to the team, the long-time maintainers and every contributor who helped make this happen. Let’s build! 💛🧡💚

items.content:
Announcing the Artificial Analysis Diarization Index, our new benchmark for who said what in speech to text

The Diarization Index scores APIs on Word Diarization Error Rate (WDER): the share of words given to the wrong speaker or to no speaker, across 97 conversations of two to eight people, with equal weight on each group size.

Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe from @NVIDIAAI  leads at 3.3%, ahead of Voxtral Small Transcribe 3 at 7.5%. Thread below 🧵

items.content:
Back in 2012, AlexNet was trained on two NVIDIA gaming GPUs. Jensen understodd what that meant before almost anyone else, and bet the company on it.

A couple weeks ago he spent a good chunk of a meeting with us nerding out on our little $400 open-source microrobot. Why it runs hot, which chip would get more FLOPs, how many watts it would draw 🤓

His latest big bet has been open models, his very first post on X 👇

If open models had only one champion, this week would have been the end. They have millions of builders, including plenty inside NVIDIA who’ve been messaging us the same thing: keep building in the open.

We will.

items.content:
Tencent's Hy4 ranks #3 on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index and #1 on CWE-Bench-AA

items.title: Model Specs have been a instrument that many chunks of the AI community agree are a great tool for o...
items.content:
Model Specs have been a instrument that many chunks of the AI community agree are a great tool for organizational alignment and lightweight external oversight. Still, as they're becoming more important as agents act more independently on our behalf (instead of just writing text which we use), there has been little policy facing work on what they are, how they should be used, and where the technical research community is moving with them.

I am very happy to have gotten to advise this project with contributors from both the Western and Chinese AI ecosystems. We're tarting to build more momentum around character training work that relates to this at Trillium Labs! 

One big goal I still have around all of this work is convincing more companies to release their specs and proactively manage developer relations with them. They keep leaking out of models and companies should have more pressure to release these documents.

Big credit to Edward at the Safe AI Forum for leading this across many stakeholders. Not easy to do!

items.title: @kushalbyatnal candidly, i'm surprised about the coodinated pushback here (outside of the fact that ...
items.content:
@kushalbyatnal candidly, i'm surprised about the coodinated pushback here (outside of the fact that we all have our own benchmarks, so it's fair to call out bias etc.).

Our team has spent an insane number of hours on ParseBench-2. This thing could've been released like 2-3 months ago as "benchmark slop" purely for marketing purposes, but we spent lot of effort tuning both our annotations and metrics to be a lot more fair to competitors compared to ParseBench-1. There were some legitimate annotation and metric issues on ParseBench-1, and actually with ParseBench-2 it actually highlights everyone in a better light! 
For instance: 
- you guys (Extend) take the top spot on forms relative to price
- Datalab does well on tables relative to price
- Reducto r-1 does well on charts relative to price (we fixed the score here) 

I'm fine if folks criticize the benchmark - there are actually annotation issues we're working on, and we're all technically competing - but I will strongly push back on any attacks on our credibility. It is absolutely unfair to call this marketing slop anymore than any other benchmark isn't marketing slop. 

We use these benchmarks for our own understanding of capabilities, we've documented our learnings in the tech report, everything is open-source, and we're shipping fixes in metrics/annotations as we speak. 

It's also actually updated over time, so we are very happy to update the rankings as new releases come out, as we've seen from others.

items.title: You shouldn’t blindly trust benchmarks - you should be able to encode your preferences relative to y...
items.content:
You shouldn’t blindly trust benchmarks - you should be able to encode your preferences relative to your use cases and design eval metrics around that.

We’re excited to release ParseBench-2 as not only a comprehensive document parsing benchmark, but also a framework for parsing benchmark design. Where you can articulate a set of human preferences of what “good parsing” looks like and “hillclimb” evaluation metrics against that.

The important part is not hand-crafting a deterministic parsing metric. Metric design can be automated by coding agents; what’s important is an open framework + datasets for encoding human preferences and optimizing metrics.

📋 For instance, if you’re dealing with mostly backoffice data, you may care about accurate form parsing, bounding boxes, and scans!

📊 On the other hand, if you’re dealing with investor research reports, you may care more about tables and charts, but less around handwriting.

We let you encode a severity policy that encodes the impact of every negative parsing error, and forces the metric to fit against it - think of fitting a linear regression in high-dimensional space.

A baseline approach for encoding human preferences is LLM as a judge. But the result of this approach vs. a “simple” LLM as a judge call is that you get much more granular, repeatable, quantifiable breakdowns of each dimension that are efficiently run at scale.

For instance, one OCR tool might be better at linearizing text, but worse at preserving formatting. Another OCR tool might be better at preserving empty rows in tables but struggle with merged cells.

The scores reflected on our website do reflect a “default” preference, but it is explicitly and transparently articulated both in our Github and technical report. The important part is that you can change and customize it for your needs.

ParseBench-2 is our most ambitious, comprehensive open benchmark to date. It is not simply a set of deterministic metrics, but a framework for designing parse evals.

We’re rapidly working on improvements and expansions (e.g. fixing minor annotation issues and tuning metrics). If you have thoughts please chime in! Everything is fully OSS.

ParseBench-2 Blog: https://t.co/6ZsSDGAiVB
Technical Report: https://t.co/f6SxkKIlme

items.title: There are thousands of OCR tools out there, and ParseBench-2 represents our attempt to not only buil...
items.content:
There are thousands of OCR tools out there, and ParseBench-2 represents our attempt to not only build a standardized benchmark, but a framework for understanding which tools do better on which dimensions. 

On day 1, we’ve benchmarked 40 different tools across 6 different dimensions:
* specialized OCR tools
* frontier models
* open-weight solutions

We’ve aggressively tried to improve the metrics from ParseBench-1 to reflect real penalties while remaining quantitative.

*** For what it’s worth, I would take the overall score with a grain of salt, since it’s a simple composite average. A lot of the insights/nuances in the benchmark come from analyzing each individual dimension and understanding the tagging behind each failure case.

It’s fascinating to see where models and other vendors do well - we don’t top the charts in every dimension relative to price point!

✅ frontier models are hillclimbing certain dimensions while ignoring others. e.g. opus 5.5 is quite good at tables, while bad at charts

✅ specialized OCR providers do well on various dimensions, e.g. Extend on forms, Datalab on tables, (we also fixed reducto r-1 chart evals)

There has been some feedback on annotations and metrics that we’re continuing to take into account, and will create new versions soon.

Also reminder that if you care about certain errors more than others, you're welcome to customize the severities for the use cases you care about. 

We’re going to be adding a ton more models to the leaderboard, come check it out: https://t.co/PWczfhp0OX

Hugging Face: https://t.co/T1FLO2V2xd

He cautions the composite score hides nuance and notes frontier models hillclimb some dimensions (e.g., Opus 5.5 strong at tables) while ignoring others.
items.content_html:
There are thousands of OCR tools out there, and ParseBench-2 represents our attempt to not only build a standardized benchmark, but a framework for understanding which tools do better on which dimensions.

On day 1, we’ve benchmarked 40 different tools across 6 different dimensions:

* specialized OCR tools

* frontier models

* open-weight solutions

We’ve aggressively tried to improve the metrics from ParseBench-1 to reflect real penalties while remaining quantitative.

*** For what it’s worth, I would take the overall score with a grain of salt, since it’s a simple composite average. A lot of the insights/nuances in the benchmark come from analyzing each individual dimension and understanding the tagging behind each failure case.

It’s fascinating to see where models and other vendors do well - we don’t top the charts in every dimension relative to price point!

✅ frontier models are hillclimbing certain dimensions while ignoring others. e.g. opus 5.5 is quite good at tables, while bad at charts

✅ specialized OCR providers do well on various dimensions, e.g. Extend on forms, Datalab on tables, (we also fixed reducto r-1 chart evals)

There has been some feedback on annotations and metrics that we’re continuing to take into account, and will create new versions soon.

Also reminder that if you care about certain errors more than others, you're welcome to customize the severities for the use cases you care about.

We’re going to be adding a ton more models to the leaderboard, come check it out: https://t.co/PWczfhp0OX

items.title: H3-Image Highspeed generates images about 1.3x to 1.4x faster than H3-Image and 1.6x to 1.7x the pri...
items.content:
H3-Image Highspeed generates images about 1.3x to 1.4x faster than H3-Image and 1.6x to 1.7x the price

MiniMax released H3-Image on November 10 as an open weights model that uses the architecture of its H3 video model with the audio layers removed. H3-Image Highspeed, which MiniMax describes as a high-speed version of H3-Image, is available on its API only. We benchmarked both on the MiniMax API at 1K resolution with prompt enhancement on, the API default.

➤ Speed: in Text to Image, Highspeed's median generation time in our hourly speed benchmark is 8.8 seconds, against 11.7 for H3-Image. In Image Editing, in a 10-prompt test, it took 10.3 seconds against 14.7.

➤ Price: H3-Image costs $21.79 per 1k images for Text to Image and $26.54 for Image Editing. H3-Image Highspeed costs $35.29 and $45.25.

➤ Availability: H3-Image is available through the MiniMax API, Hailuo AI and MiniMax Code, and H3-Image Highspeed through the MiniMax API.

➤ Licence: H3-Image's weights are on Hugging Face under the MiniMax-H3-Image Community License. It excludes the EU, the UK, South Korea and the US, and requires MiniMax's written permission for companies above $1M in annual revenue or for hosted services.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: The FAA just stopped every departing flight in the US, only the 2nd nationwide ...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: The FAA just stopped every departing flight in the US, only the 2nd nationwide ground stop since 9/11.

• Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed "a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," the 22 centers that handle flights above 18,000 feet
• About 3,100 aircraft were in the air when it hit, and nearly 7,000 flights have been delayed or canceled
• DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin called it "a telecommunication outage" and said there's no sign of a "nefarious attack"
• Hours before the outage, the White House and DOT asked Congress for another $30.1B to modernize air traffic control, on top of $12.5B approved last year

@theojaffee: "This is extremely rare. This has only happened in history twice. The first time was 9/11. The second time was 2023, when the FAA's NOTAM system went down."

items.content:
This is a really good test for agents:

It's a benchmark released by Deepnote. (I've used their platform for 5+ years and I love it!)

The benchmark tests agents in a simulated company's Slack:

• Agents get access to records across 11 services
• They face 50 different situations
• They have 3 minutes to investigate and decide

Here is what they test:

1. Does the agent know when to help?
2. Does the agent know how to help accurately?
3. Does the agent know when to stay quiet?

items.title: In Text to Image, H3-Image comes closest to the leaders in Human Anatomy and Knowledge, and is clear...
items.content:
In Text to Image, H3-Image comes closest to the leaders in Human Anatomy and Knowledge, and is clearly ahead of models at its level on Layout

Our Image Arena taxonomy measures 9 capabilities and 10 use cases for Text to Image. Capabilities measure the skills a prompt tests.

H3-Image trails GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst (max) by 149 Elo in Human Anatomy and 160 in Knowledge, and GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) by 269 in Text Rendering. Text to Image is its weaker board: every gap here is wider than any of its gaps in Image Editing.

Against models at its level, it is clearly ahead of Krea 2 Large and MAI-Image-2.5-Flash on Layout, and clearly behind Qwen-Image-3.0 and Qwen-Image-3.0-Pro on Text Rendering.

➤ Human Anatomy covers hands, faces, body proportion, dynamic poses and movement.

➤ Knowledge covers real landmarks, species, and domain facts across science and common sense.

➤ Layout covers flows, arrows, blocks, visual hierarchy and multi-panel compositions.

H3-Image is 43 Elo behind GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) on Enhancement & Restoration, within the margin of error, and 56 behind GPT Image 2.6 Flare (max) on Reasoning-Based Edit. Its widest gap is Text or Symbol Edits, 119 Elo behind GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max). Reasoning-Based Edit and Composition & Framing are also where it leads other open weights models most clearly.

H3-Image Highspeed (dotted line) has the same profile: on every editing action, the two models are within the margin of error of each other.

➤ Enhancement & Restoration covers denoising, retouching, artifact removal, and repair of damaged or degraded images.

➤ Reasoning-Based Edit covers edits that require inference about the scene rather than a literal instruction.

➤ Composition & Framing covers cropping, extending, reframing, and changes to camera view or perspective.

➤ Text or Symbol Edits covers editing text, typography, logos, and symbols within the image.

items.content:
This is really big for agentic evaluations!

If you aren't familiar, the Specialized Intelligence Index (SII) is a collection of tests and leaderboards to evaluate different models on domain-specific tasks.

You can find benchmarks across many domains, like reviewing contracts, answering customer questions, and writing code.

To pick the best model for a job, you can use the SII to evaluate cost, speed, and quality.

@FireworksAI_HQ is adding 31 new partners to the SII, so the number of tests will continue growing!
